result: A post-before-pre pairing protocol (postsynaptic spike 18ms before presynaptic stimulation, 100 pairings at 0.2 Hz) induced robust t-LTD at both LPP-GC synapses (63±5%, n=14) and MPP-GC synapses (59±5%, n=14), while unpaired control pathways remained unaffected (103±4% and 105±7%, respectively).
evaluation: Claims C4-C7 provide converging evidence from paired and unpaired pathways showing robust and pathway-specific t-LTD induction. The control pathways demonstrate specificity of the effect. Sample sizes are adequate (n=14) and the magnitude of depression is substantial (~40% reduction).

result: GABAA and GABAB receptor blockers (bicuculline 10 µM and SCH50911 20 µM) did not affect t-LTD at LPP-GC or MPP-GC synapses, indicating these receptors are not necessary for t-LTD induction.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9 show that GABA receptor blockade does not prevent t-LTD (LPP-GC: control 67±6% vs. blockers 69±11%; MPP-GC: control 65±8% vs. blockers 75±9%, n=6 each). The similar magnitudes of depression in control and blocker conditions support the conclusion.

result: Multiple lines of evidence demonstrate presynaptic expression of t-LTD at both LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses: increased failure rates (LPP: 43±7% to 76±6%, n=8; MPP: 40±5% to 59±4%, n=6), increased PPR (LPP: 1.16±0.11 to 1.67±0.19; MPP: 1.17±0.11 to 1.81±0.15, n=14), CV analysis consistent with release parameter changes, decreased mEPSP frequency (LPP: 1.4±0.13 to 0.7±0.09 Hz, n=6; MPP: 1.2±0.1 to 0.7±0.07 Hz, n=8) without changes in mEPSP amplitude.
evaluation: Claims C10-C23 provide four independent lines of evidence (failure analysis, PPR, CV analysis, mEPSP frequency/amplitude) all converging on a presynaptic locus. The consistency across multiple approaches, adequate sample sizes, and lack of postsynaptic amplitude changes strongly support presynaptic expression. However, CV analysis has known limitations in CNS synapses (acknowledged by authors), and the R² values are relatively low (0.337 and 0.168).

result: t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses requires ionotropic, non-postsynaptic NMDARs, while t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses does not require NMDARs. Bath-applied D-AP5 (50 µM) and MK-801 (500 µM) blocked t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses (90±7% and 107±10%, respectively, vs. control 60±7%) but not at LPP-GC synapses (66±4% and 62±9% vs. control 60±6%). Postsynaptic loading of MK-801 did not block MPP-GC t-LTD (54±7%).
evaluation: Claims C24-C30 demonstrate a clear differential requirement for NMDARs between the two synapse types. The bath vs. postsynaptic loading experiment (C27-C28) provides strong evidence for non-postsynaptic (likely presynaptic) NMDARs at MPP-GC synapses. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-10) and the blocking effect is complete.

result: The presynaptic NMDARs required for t-LTD at MPP-GC synapses contain GluN2A subunits. Zn²⁺ (300 nM), a GluN2A antagonist, completely blocked t-LTD (95±5%, n=7), while antagonists of GluN2B (Ro25-6981: 55±11%, n=6; ifenprodil: 62±11%, n=6) and GluN2C/2D (PPDA: 61±7%, n=6) did not affect t-LTD (control: 63±6%, n=9).
evaluation: Claims C31-C35 use pharmacological subunit-specific antagonists to identify GluN2A-containing NMDARs. The complete block by Zn²⁺ and lack of effect by other antagonists provide strong evidence. However, pharmacological specificity is not absolute, and the conclusion would be strengthened by genetic approaches.

result: Both LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses require mGluR activity for t-LTD, but with different subtype requirements: LPP-GC synapses require mGluR5 (blocked by MPEP: 103±10%, n=8, but not by LY367385: 76±3%, n=6), while MPP-GC synapses require mGluR1 (blocked by LY367385: 95±7%, n=7, but not by MPEP: 61±7%, n=6). The broad-spectrum antagonist LY341495 blocked t-LTD at both synapse types (LPP: 100±10%, n=8; MPP: 99±9%, n=10).
evaluation: Claims C36-C42 demonstrate differential mGluR subtype requirements using selective antagonists. The reciprocal pattern (mGluR5 for LPP, mGluR1 for MPP) is clear and well-controlled with interleaved controls. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-10).

result: t-LTD at both LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses requires postsynaptic Ca²⁺ release from ryanodine-sensitive intracellular stores, but not L-type Ca²⁺ channels or IP3 receptors. Nimodipine (10 µM) did not prevent t-LTD (LPP: 79±4%, n=6; MPP: 67±6%, n=6). Thapsigargin (1-10 µM) prevented t-LTD when applied in bath or loaded postsynaptically (LPP: 108±16% and 107±7%; MPP: 108±6% and 98±4%). Heparin (5 mg/ml) did not prevent t-LTD (LPP: 77±8%; MPP: 81±10%, n=6), but ruthenium red prevented t-LTD (LPP: 98±12%, n=7; MPP: 98±12%, n=6).
evaluation: Claims C43-C56 systematically dissect Ca²⁺ sources using multiple pharmacological tools. The pattern is consistent: thapsigargin and ruthenium red block t-LTD, while nimodipine and heparin do not, pointing to ryanodine receptors. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-15). However, the specificity of ruthenium red for ryanodine receptors has been questioned, and the high concentration of thapsigargin may have off-target effects.

result: Postsynaptic calcineurin is required for t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses but not at MPP-GC synapses. Bath-applied FK506 (10 µM) prevented t-LTD at LPP-GC (110±7%, n=8) but not MPP-GC synapses (72±7%, n=6). Postsynaptic loading of FK506 (1-10 µM) also prevented t-LTD at LPP-GC synapses (109±8%, n=13).
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 demonstrate differential calcineurin requirements using bath and postsynaptic application of FK506. The complete block at LPP-GC and lack of effect at MPP-GC is clear. The postsynaptic loading experiment confirms the locus. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-13).

result: Both forms of t-LTD require endocannabinoid (eCB) synthesis and CB1 receptor activation. Postsynaptic loading of THL (5 µM) to block eCB synthesis prevented t-LTD at both LPP-GC (92±7%, n=8) and MPP-GC synapses (92±5%, n=6). The CB1R antagonist AM251 (3 µM) blocked t-LTD at both synapse types (LPP: 102±7%, n=14; MPP: 98±5%, n=6). Direct CB1R activation by WIN 55,212-2 (10 µM) puffs induced LTD at both synapse types (LPP: 83±9%, n=6; MPP: 79±3%, n=6).
evaluation: Claims C61-C67 provide three lines of evidence for eCB/CB1R involvement: blocking synthesis (THL), blocking receptors (AM251), and direct receptor activation (WIN). The consistency across approaches is strong. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-14). However, the location of CB1Rs (neuronal vs. astrocytic) is not definitively established.

result: Astrocytes and Ca²⁺-dependent vesicular release are required for t-LTD at both LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses. Loading astrocytes with BAPTA (20 mM) impaired t-LTD (LPP: 103±9%, n=6; MPP: 94±6%, n=6). t-LTD was absent in dnSNARE mice (LPP: 102±9%, n=9; MPP: 112±6%, n=7) compared to WT controls (LPP: 71±5%, n=7; MPP: 60±5%, n=6). Loading astrocytes with tetanus toxin light chain (TeTxLC, 1 µM) impaired t-LTD (LPP: 106±9%, n=6; MPP: 108±10%, n=6).
evaluation: Claims C68-C74 use four independent approaches (BAPTA loading, dnSNARE mice, TeTxLC, and later glutamate rescue) to demonstrate astrocyte requirement. The convergence of evidence is strong. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-9). The dnSNARE mouse model is well-validated in the literature.

result: Glutamate released via SNARE-dependent exocytosis by astrocytes is necessary for t-LTD induction. Loading astrocytes with Evans blue (5 µM) to block vesicular glutamate uptake impaired t-LTD (LPP: 106±6%, n=6; MPP: 106±11%, n=6). Glutamate puffs (100 µM) rescued t-LTD in dnSNARE mice (LPP: 72±11%, n=6; MPP: 70±8%, n=6) to levels comparable to WT controls (LPP: 62±8%, n=7; MPP: 64±5%, n=7).
evaluation: Claims C75-C79 provide strong evidence for astrocytic glutamate by blocking its release (Evans blue) and rescuing the phenotype in dnSNARE mice with exogenous glutamate. The rescue experiment is particularly compelling. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-7). However, Evans blue specificity for VGLUT has been questioned, and glutamate puffs may activate receptors non-physiologically.

result: Two novel forms of presynaptic t-LTD were discovered at LPP-GC and MPP-GC synapses, both requiring postsynaptic Ca²⁺, eCB synthesis, CB1R activation, and astrocytic glutamate release, but differing in their requirements for NMDARs (MPP only, GluN2A-containing), mGluRs (mGluR5 for LPP, mGluR1 for MPP), and calcineurin (LPP only).
evaluation: Claims C80-C87 and C103-C108 summarize the main findings. The evidence from individual experiments (covered in previous results) collectively supports these summary statements. The differential molecular requirements between LPP and MPP synapses are well-established through systematic pharmacological dissection.

result: Background knowledge claims about EC-hippocampus connectivity, functional differences between LPP and MPP, pathological involvement in disease, and general principles of synaptic plasticity and STDP.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C88-C102 represent established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited. These provide context for the experimental findings but are not novel results of this study.
